subject: Agriculture
title: Farming and Climate Change
description: A micro-lesson that makes Farming and Climate Change usable.

hook.text: Agriculture produces about 10% of global greenhouse emissions—and climate change threatens agriculture back.

buildup.text: Methane from livestock, nitrous oxide from fertilizers, and CO2 from machinery all contribute.

discovery.text: Meanwhile, rising temperatures shift growing zones. Crops that thrived for centuries struggle in new weather.

twist.text: Some regions gain—Canada and Russia see longer growing seasons. Others lose—tropical yields are falling.

climax.text: Farming must cut emissions while adapting to a climate it helped create. The challenge is circular.

punchline.text: Agriculture warms the planet. The warm planet reshapes agriculture.

quiz.question: What share of global greenhouse gas emissions does agriculture produce?

details.summary: Agriculture is both a major contributor to climate change and one of its biggest victims. This topic covers farming's greenhouse gas emissions, the impacts of warming and extreme weather on crops, and how agriculture can adapt and mitigate its climate footprint.
details.whyItMatters: Agriculture accounts for about 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions while being uniquely vulnerable to the climate changes those emissions cause. Managing this paradox is critical for food security.
takeaways: Agriculture produces about 10% of global emissions from methane, nitrous oxide, and CO₂
Climate change is shifting growing zones, intensifying droughts, and increasing crop losses
Climate-smart practices can reduce emissions while maintaining or increasing food production

faq.question: How does agriculture contribute to climate change?
faq.answer: Farming emits methane from livestock and rice paddies, nitrous oxide from fertilized soils, and CO₂ from land clearing and machinery. Together, agriculture and related land use change account for roughly a quarter of global emissions.

faq.question: How is climate change affecting crop production?
faq.answer: Rising temperatures reduce yields in tropical regions, extreme weather events devastate harvests, shifting rainfall patterns disrupt planting, and pests and diseases are moving into new areas. Some temperate regions may temporarily benefit from longer seasons.
